findings.text: The first sentence says plainly what Athena is. A newcomer can repeat it after one read.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: The page says why Athena matters, and names who it is for and what they get: a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict.
findings.source: "It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The header links straight to Next steps. That section gives the clone command, the prerequisites, `./setup.sh` and a first `athena ask` command. A newcomer knows what to do next without reading the long study.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of another project, firstmate. The page explains why it is there, but a newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past many screens of firstmate internals (exit codes, places-held, teardown guards) before reaching the install steps again.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The page names cost, the two models and the verdict as Athena's selling points, but this sample study shows none of them. Nothing says which models wrote or checked it, what it cost, or what verdict it got. The demo misses the very things the lede promises.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This header link is for the project owner, not a newcomer. It sits right beside the newcomer's next step with no explanation, which could confuse a first-time reader.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Athena is described as written in Rust, but the prerequisites never mention a Rust toolchain. They also don't say which operating systems are supported. The page may be relying on setup.sh to install Rust, but it doesn't say so, so a newcomer can't tell whether their machine is ready.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)."

findings.text: The try-it step doesn't say which repository `athena ask` acts on, presumably the current directory. It also doesn't say whether it commits changes, which matters before a newcomer runs it on real code.
findings.source: "press Enter to run it on your repository"

findings.text: The page says openly that nothing was run and that a first reading missed several paths. This honesty supports the page's claim to traceability, though a newcomer may find it more inside detail than they need.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "This study read the pinned tree only... every claim is marked read."
